in_context.text: This verse is a short personal aside in the middle of Paul's instructions to Timothy about elders. Just before it, Paul tells Timothy to be careful in appointing leaders and to "keep thyself pure" (5:22). Right after it, he returns to the subject of how people's sins and good works come to light (5:24-25).

speaker.text: Paul the apostle, who names himself as the writer of the letter. Many critical scholars think a follower wrote it in Paul's name.

audience.text: Timothy, Paul's younger co-worker and "own son in the faith," whom Paul had left to lead the church at Ephesus.

affected.text: Timothy himself. The advice concerns his own stomach and his frequent illnesses, not the church as a whole.

what.text: Paul tells Timothy to stop drinking only water and to take a little wine for his stomach and his frequent ailments. It is health advice for a man who was often sick.

events.text: The advice comes while Timothy is leading the church in Ephesus after Paul left him there and went on to Macedonia.

written.text: Traditional view: about AD 62-64, by Paul, between his first and second Roman imprisonments. Scholarly view: many critical scholars date it around AD 80-110 and see it as written in Paul's name by a follower; others defend the earlier date and Paul's authorship.

where.text: Timothy was in Ephesus, a wealthy port city and capital of the Roman province of Asia. The letter does not say where it was written; Paul may have been in Macedonia.

purpose.text: Paul cares for Timothy's health as well as his leadership. The verse follows the command "keep thyself pure" (5:22), but the text does not explain exactly how the two are linked.

big_picture.text: The letter teaches that "every creature of God is good" when received with thanksgiving (4:4). It also warns that leaders must not be "given to wine" or "much wine" (3:3, 3:8). This verse fits both: a little wine for health, not heavy drinking.

for_readers.text: Faithful service and caring for the body are not at odds. Paul gives practical, limited advice to a sick friend. He does not lay down a general rule about drinking.

misuse.popular_reading: Quoted as a general Bible endorsement of drinking alcohol, as if Paul tells everyone to drink wine.

in_context_reading.text: In context it is personal advice to one man, Timothy, who was drinking only water and was often ill. Paul says "a little" wine, and only "for thy stomach's sake and thine often infirmities." The same letter warns leaders against being given to wine.

why_it_matters.text: The Greek word means to be a water-drinker, the opposite of using wine. Paul is not telling Timothy to give up water. He is telling him to stop drinking water only.
The word means a small or slight amount. This limits the advice to a modest quantity.
The word means weakness, frailty, or sickness, and here it is plural. Together with "often" (G4437, frequent), it shows the reason was Timothy's repeated illness.
In later Greek writers this word means the stomach. The advice is tied to a specific bodily complaint, not to pleasure or celebration.

takeaway.text: This is a caring, practical word from Paul to a sick co-worker: drink a little wine, not only water, for your health. It is not a blanket command for all believers, and the same letter warns against heavy drinking.

resolved.reason: Kourtland (2026-10-23): when the text and its context are clear, answer from Scripture instead of noting that Christians disagree.
resolved.fix: hedge removed; answered from the text and other Scripture
